aio_response.text:
When the Federal Reserve raises interest rates, it increases borrowing costs and cools overall economic demand, which helps drive inflation down toward its 2% target.

How Rate Increases Affect Inflation

• Higher Borrowing Costs: Raising the federal funds rate causes commercial banks to increase prime lending rates, making mortgages, auto loans, credit cards, and business lines of credit more expensive.
• Dampened Consumer and Business Spending: Because borrowing costs rise, households cut back on large purchases and businesses scale back investments and expansions. This drop in aggregate demand reduces upward pressure on prices.
• Increased Incentives to Save: Higher rates boost yields on savings accounts, certificates of deposit (CDs), and money market funds, encouraging people to save rather than spend.
• Sector-Specific Impact: Interest-sensitive sectors—such as housing and auto manufacturing—react most sharply and quickly to rate hikes, while service-sector inflation often takes longer to adjust.
• Time Lags: Policy changes do not work immediately; there is a notable economic lag—often months—between a Fed rate hike and its full effect showing up in inflation data.

Official Resources & Guides

• Review the Federal Reserve Monetary Policy FAQ to learn how the central bank uses interest rates to balance employment and price stability.
• Read the Cleveland Fed Inflation Guide for a deeper breakdown of the dual mandate and the 2% target.
